summary: This program defines a RobotPet class whose battery level is guarded by a property, so the value can never fall below 0 or rise above 100. It then walks and charges the pet named Rover to show the guard at work.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery inside __init__ goes through the property setter rather than storing the number directly, so even a bad starting value gets corrected.
The @property decorator turns the method below it into an attribute that is read with pet.battery, without parentheses.
The real value lives in _battery, and the leading underscore is the convention that marks it as internal to the class.
This decorator registers the next method as the code that runs whenever something assigns to pet.battery.
Any attempt to drop below empty is caught here and stored as 0 instead.
Likewise, a value above a full charge is capped at 100, which is what clamping means.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring states the method's purpose in the code itself, where help() and editors can find it.
The cost of a walk is worked out from a single rule, so changing the drain rate means editing one number.
The comparison itself evaluates to True or False, so there is no need for an if statement here.
Subtracting from self.battery still passes through the setter, so the battery cannot go negative.
Creating an instance runs __init__ with these arguments and gives back an object stored in pet1.
Asking before acting is the point of can_walk: the program checks feasibility, then commits to the walk.
A 50-minute walk would cost 100% battery, which Rover no longer has, so this run takes the else branch.
Adding 40 to a battery of 65 would give 105, but the setter clamps the result to 100.
